name: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome
aliases: Familial atypical mole and melanoma syndrome

clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant predisposition defined by numerous melanocytic naevi, several of them clinically atypical, together with a strong family history of cutaneous melanoma.
Most commonly caused by germline mutations in CDKN2A on the short arm of chromosome 9; a minority of families carry CDK4 mutations.

CDKN2A encodes two distinct tumour-suppressor proteins from overlapping reading frames: p16 (INK4a), which restrains CDK4 and CDK6 within the retinoblastoma pathway, and p14 (ARF), which stabilises p53.
The lifetime risk of cutaneous melanoma is very high, often with early onset and multiple primary melanomas.
CDKN2A carriers, particularly in certain families, have a markedly increased risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and some show excess risk of other tumours.
Naevi vary in size and colour with irregular borders, so new, changing or symptomatic lesions warrant a low threshold for dermoscopy and excision.

Management centres on rigorous photoprotection, structured self-examination, regular dermatological surveillance with total-body photography and dermoscopy, and consideration of pancreatic surveillance in gene carriers.
reference.pathophysiology: The CDKN2A locus on the short arm of chromosome 9 is unusual in encoding two unrelated tumour-suppressor proteins through alternative first exons and reading frames. p16 (INK4a) inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6, preventing phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein and thereby holding cells at the G1 to S transition; loss of p16 releases this brake and permits unchecked proliferation. p14 (ARF) sequesters MDM2, stabilising p53 and preserving apoptosis and senescence in response to oncogenic stress, so its loss impairs p53-mediated tumour suppression. Germline inactivation of one CDKN2A allele, combined with somatic loss of the second and cumulative ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in melanocytes, drives melanoma formation and explains the early onset and multiple primary tumours. Because the same pathway operates in pancreatic ductal epithelium, loss of p16 also predisposes to pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Rare CDK4 mutations act differently, rendering the kinase resistant to inhibition by p16 and producing a similar melanoma-prone phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic multiple or atypical (dysplastic) naevi without a germline predisposition
BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome with melanoma and other tumours
Xeroderma pigmentosum with ultraviolet sensitivity and cutaneous malignancy
Familial melanoma associated with other loci such as MITF or POT1
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome for the mucocutaneous pigmented lesion differential
Sporadic melanoma arising outside a familial context
additionalInvestigations: Germline testing for CDKN2A and CDK4 mutations with genetic counselling
Whole-skin examination with dermoscopy and total-body photography for surveillance
Excisional biopsy and histopathology of suspicious pigmented lesions
Pancreatic surveillance with endoscopic ultrasound and MRI-MRCP in appropriate gene carriers
Documentation of naevus count and atypia with sequential monitoring for change
Ophthalmological review where ocular pigmented lesions are noted
redFlags: A pigmented lesion changing in size, shape or colour, or one that bleeds or ulcerates
A new nodular or amelanotic lesion in a high-risk individual
Features suggesting pancreatic malignancy such as painless jaundice, new-onset diabetes or unexplained weight loss
Lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms suggesting metastatic melanoma
reference.prognosis: With vigilant surveillance many melanomas are detected early and cured by excision, but the cumulative lifetime melanoma risk is high and the associated pancreatic cancer risk carries a poor outlook. Adherence to lifelong surveillance is therefore important.
pitfalls: Reassuring a patient on the basis of a single normal skin check rather than instituting ongoing surveillance
Focusing only on skin cancer risk and neglecting counselling about pancreatic cancer in CDKN2A carriers
Assuming that a negative genetic test excludes the syndrome, since not all familial melanoma is explained by known genes
Under-recognising amelanotic or nodular melanoma among numerous benign naevi
references: Clinical genetics and hereditary cancer references
management: Lifelong whole-skin surveillance with dermoscopy and total-body photography, with a low threshold for excisional biopsy of new or changing pigmented lesions
Wide local excision of confirmed cutaneous melanoma, with sentinel node assessment and immunotherapy or BRAF/MEK-targeted therapy reserved for advanced disease
Rigorous photoprotection with sun avoidance, protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen, and avoidance of artificial tanning
Patient education in structured regular skin self-examination
Pancreatic cancer surveillance with endoscopic ultrasound and MRI-MRCP in appropriate CDKN2A carriers
Genetic counselling with germline CDKN2A and CDK4 testing and cascade screening of relatives
Coordinated dermatology, clinical genetics and, where relevant, hepatobiliary multidisciplinary care
